newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: BLACK JCI CAN'T BUCK TREND ON JOB CUTS.
newsitem.headline: BLACK JCI CAN'T BUCK TREND ON JOB CUTS.

text.p: JCI Ltd's new management might be black and symbolise economic empowerment but its decision on Wednesday to retrench a third of struggling Randfontein Gold Mining Co's workforce was business as usual.
Analysts said that the South African mining house's first black chairman Mzi Khumalo had no choice but to reduce Randfontein's workforce if he wanted to save the gold mine.

Randfontein's slide into a 2.8 million rand loss for the three months to March, from a 43.8 million rand profit in the previous quarter, was due to falling production, compounded by the current sickly bullion price.

"Absolutely (it was a sound business decision). He's got to get that mine back on track. This should pull it right but it's not a very happy situation," said Leon Esterhuizen, analyst at South Africa's SocGen Frankel Pollak.
JCI announced earlier on Wednesday that it planned to shed between 3,400 and 4,100 Randfontein jobs and cut tonnage throughput as part of a far-reaching restructuring programme.
Retrenchments would take place on May 31.
The black National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), while shocked and disappointed, did not lambast Khumalo personally, laying the blame squarely on the shoulders of the mining house.
"We are not dealing with an individual here. We are dealing with a company. He (Khumalo) is doing his job," said NUM national spokesman George Molebatsi.
"The mining company has its own policy of dealing with the union and it cannot change overnight. An individual cannot determine the policy of an entire company," he said.
But NUM Randfontein mine spokesman, Thabani Mngomezulu, was not as forgiving.

"Capital does not know the colour of the skin. Mzi Khumalo has to do what he has to do but the workers have lost faith in him," he said earlier in the week when rumours of the big job cuts first surfaced.

Khumalo -- South Africa's first black "randlord" -- took the reins of one of the world's biggest gold miners after black empowerment consortium African Mining Group, led by him, bought 34.9 percent of JCI last year.
Analysts say Khumalo, having successfully broken into one of South Africa's white bastions, has unfortunately inherited a business suffering severely from production problems.
"You're looking at a business that's dying and if it does no-one has a job," said Esterhuizen.
South African gold mines announced disappointing March quarter results, mostly due to the gold price fall. But the poor performance is part of an enduring trend.
National output fell to 494.6 tonnes last year -- the lowest since the 1950s, while working costs have soared to an average 43,367 rand per kg of gold mined from 505 rand/kg in 1950.

"Randfontein is very much a sign of the times. The threat of job cuts has been there for some time. It's the nature of mining that when the gold price falls, pay (profitably mined) areas are reduced," said Dave Giese, analyst at Smith Borkhum Hare.
Mines statistics show that the number of workers employed on gold mines has fallen sharply to 342,439 by the end of 1996 from 505,262 in 1986.
The NUM said that the Randfontein job cuts were too large.
"It came as a surprise. We got notification about a month ago and we wanted to talk about restructuring before retrenchments. This is far too many people," Molebatsi said.
JCI said that as a result of the restructuring the tonnage throughput would be reduced to allow for more optimal mining of the orebody at an increased grade.
"Management regrets the need to reduce the workforce by this large number of people, but this is essential in order to improve margins and efficiences," it said.
Randfontein produced 4,392 kg of gold in the March quarter compared to 5,100 kg in the December quarter.
Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd last month also warned of shaft closures and job cuts at its Free State Consolidated Gold Mine Ltd and Vaal Reefs Exploration and Mining Co Ltd .
